lead: Superdense coding sends two classical bits to a receiver while physically sending only one qubit. The extra bit is not free: Alice and Bob must share one entangled Bell pair before the protocol starts. Alice encodes her two bits by applying one of four single-qubit gates to her half of the pair, then mails that qubit to Bob. Bob runs a CNOT and a Hadamard and measures both qubits. The scheme is used wherever a link already shares entanglement and wants more classical payload per qubit sent, and as a laboratory test that a device really produces Bell pairs.
prereq: You need 3.1 for the Pauli gates X, Z and the Hadamard gate H, 3.2 for CNOT, 3.4 for reading a circuit diagram left to right, and Unit 2 for Bell states and measurement.

sections.h3: One qubit, two bits: what the shared pair buys

blocks.text: Superdense coding delivers two classical bits to a receiver by physically sending one qubit. The trick needs a resource shared in advance: one Bell pair.

blocks.where: the first ket slot is Alice's qubit and the second is Bob's; the factor 1/√2 (≈ 0.7071) normalises the state so the probabilities add to 1.

blocks.text: One qubit alone cannot do this. Holevo's bound says that n qubits carry at most n classical bits of information that a receiver can actually read out. So a single qubit, with no help, delivers one bit and no more. The second bit travels inside the correlations of the pair, not inside the qubit itself.

Alice holds one half of the pair, Bob the other. Alice chooses her two bits b₁b₂ (each is 0 or 1), applies one gate to her own qubit, then sends that qubit to Bob over a quantum channel: an optical fibre, free space, or simply a wire in a circuit. Bob now holds both halves and extracts the bits with a fixed two-gate circuit followed by a measurement.

Count the resources: one ebit (one shared Bell pair) used up in advance, one qubit sent through the channel, two classical bits delivered. The ebit is consumed — after the protocol the pair no longer exists, so a second message needs a fresh pair.

items: Prepare the Bell pair |Φ+⟩. Give qubit 1 to Alice, qubit 2 to Bob.
Alice picks her two bits b₁b₂ and applies the matching gate to qubit 1 only: I for 00, X for 01, Z for 10, XZ for 11.
Alice sends qubit 1 to Bob. This is the only physical transmission in the protocol.
Bob applies CNOT with qubit 1 as control and qubit 2 as target.
Bob measures both qubits in the computational basis. The outcome on qubit 1 is b₁ and on qubit 2 is b₂.

blocks.text: The four gates are the identity I, the bit flip X, the phase flip Z, and the product XZ, read as Z first and then X. Each one turns the same starting pair into a different Bell state, and the four Bell states are mutually orthogonal. Orthogonal states can be told apart by one measurement with zero error. Alice's choice of gate is what selects which of the four states Bob receives.

The pair CNOT-then-H is the circuit that creates a Bell pair, run backwards. CNOT removes the entanglement and leaves the two qubits in a product state; H then converts any leftover phase difference into a visible difference between |0⟩ and |1⟩. Together they perform a Bell-basis measurement, dumping each Bell state onto a distinct two-bit string.

Check the Z case by hand. Z leaves |0⟩ alone and sends |1⟩ to −|1⟩, so (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 becomes (|00⟩ − |11⟩)/√2, which is Φ−. CNOT maps |11⟩ to |10⟩ and leaves |00⟩ alone, giving (|00⟩ − |10⟩)/√2 = ((|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2) ⊗ |0⟩. The H gate sends (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2 to |1⟩, so the final state is |10⟩ and Bob reads 1 then 0 — the message 10.

This is the mirror image of teleportation. There, one ebit plus two classical bits move one unknown qubit. Here, one ebit plus one qubit moves two classical bits. Same two resources, roles swapped; in both cases the entanglement is destroyed by the decoding step.

figure.caption: Sending the two bits 10: Alice's Z gate turns the shared pair into |Φ−⟩, and Bob's CNOT then H turns that into |10⟩, so he measures 1 then 0. The other three messages use I, X and XZ instead of Z.

spec.title: Worked example: sending 10
spec.aria: A top-to-bottom flowchart of the worked example: starting from |Φ+⟩, Alice applies Z to get |Φ−⟩, sends qubit 1, Bob applies CNOT to get (|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2 ⊗ |0⟩, then H to get |10⟩, and measures 1 and 0, recovering the message 10.

examples.question: Alice and Bob share the Bell pair |Φ+⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, with Alice holding qubit 1. Alice wants to send the two classical bits 10. (a) Which gate does she apply? (b) What state does Bob hold after her qubit arrives? (c) What does Bob measure after applying CNOT and then H?
steps: Read the message: b₁ = 1 and b₂ = 0.
Match against the encoding table: 00 → I, 01 → X, 10 → Z, 11 → XZ. The message 10 selects Z.
Start from the shared state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, with qubit 1 first.
Apply Z to qubit 1 only. Z|0⟩ = |0⟩ and Z|1⟩ = −|1⟩, so the state becomes (|00⟩ − |11⟩)/√2, which is |Φ−⟩.
Alice sends qubit 1 to Bob. Bob now owns both qubits and the pair is still entangled, now in |Φ−⟩.
Bob applies CNOT (control qubit 1, target qubit 2). |00⟩ is unchanged; |11⟩ becomes |10⟩. The state is (|00⟩ − |10⟩)/√2 = ((|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2) ⊗ |0⟩.
Bob applies H to qubit 1. H(|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2 = |1⟩, so the state is |1⟩ ⊗ |0⟩ = |10⟩.
Bob measures both qubits. Qubit 1 gives 1 and qubit 2 gives 0, so the recovered message is 10.
examples.answer: Alice applies Z; Bob receives |Φ−⟩, and after CNOT and H he measures qubit 1 as 1 and qubit 2 as 0, recovering the message 10.
examples.check:
bits = "10"
b1 = int(bits[0])
b2 = int(bits[1])
print(b1)
print(b2)

traps: One qubit by itself carries at most one classical bit. The second bit comes from the shared ebit, never from the qubit alone. Without a pre-shared pair the protocol does not work at all.
No classical signal is sent in this protocol. The two bits are never written as voltages, pulses or packets; the only thing that travels is Alice's single qubit.
Memorise the encoding table in the order 00 → I, 01 → X, 10 → Z, 11 → XZ. Swapping Z and XZ sends 10 and 11 to the wrong Bell states.
XZ means apply Z first and then X. Undoing the order costs a global minus sign, which changes nothing measurable, but the table entry still has to be quoted correctly.
Bob's CNOT takes Alice's qubit as control and his own as target. Reversing control and target decodes into a different, wrong bit string.

quiz.q: List the four gates Alice may apply in superdense coding and the two-bit message each one encodes.
quiz.a: I for 00, X for 01, Z for 10, XZ for 11.

quiz.q: State the resources used by superdense coding and what Bob does after he receives Alice's qubit.
quiz.a: One shared ebit before the protocol, one qubit sent, two classical bits received. Bob applies CNOT with qubit 1 as control and qubit 2 as target, then H on qubit 1, then measures both qubits.

quiz.q: Why does the protocol need the shared Bell pair? Why can Alice not just send her qubit without it?
quiz.a: By Holevo's bound one qubit alone yields at most one readable classical bit. The second bit lives in the entanglement correlations. The four gates rotate the pair into four mutually orthogonal Bell states, and orthogonality is exactly what lets Bob read both bits with zero error. Without the shared pair, the four possible states of a single qubit are not all orthogonal and carry only one bit.

quiz.q: In what sense is superdense coding the dual of quantum teleportation?
quiz.a: Teleportation moves one unknown qubit using one ebit and two classical bits. Superdense coding moves two classical bits using one ebit and one qubit. The resources are the same; the quantum and classical roles are exchanged, and in both cases the ebit is consumed.

quiz.q: Alice and Bob share |Φ+⟩. Alice wants to send 01. Which gate does she apply, what state does Bob hold, and what does he read after CNOT and H?
quiz.a: Message 01 selects X. X flips Alice's qubit, so the state becomes (|01⟩ + |10⟩)/√2 = Ψ+. CNOT gives (|01⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 = ((|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2) ⊗ |1⟩. H on qubit 1 sends (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 to |0⟩, leaving |01⟩. Bob reads 0 on qubit 1 and 1 on qubit 2 — message 01.

quiz.q: Alice sends 11. Write the state after her gate, after CNOT, and after H, and give Bob's measurement outcomes.
quiz.a: Gate XZ gives −(|01⟩ − |10⟩)/√2, which is Ψ− up to a global minus sign. CNOT maps |01⟩ to |01⟩ and |10⟩ to |11⟩, giving (|01⟩ − |11⟩)/√2 = ((|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2) ⊗ |1⟩. H on qubit 1 gives |1⟩ ⊗ |1⟩ = |11⟩. Bob measures 1 and 1 — message 11.

quiz.q: Bob forgets the H gate and applies only CNOT. Can he still recover the bits? Test with the message 00.
quiz.a: For 00 the state is (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. CNOT maps |11⟩ to |10⟩, giving (|00⟩ + |10⟩)/√2 = ((|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2) ⊗ |0⟩. Qubit 2 always reads 0, but qubit 1 reads 0 or 1 with equal probability, so the message is random. Without H the four Bell states are not mapped onto the four computational basis states; H is what converts a phase difference into a definite bit value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Superdense coding was proposed by Bennett and Wiesner in 1992 and has since been demonstrated over optical fibre and free-space links. It is a standard benchmark: if a device shows the full two-bits-per-qubit rate, its Bell pairs are genuinely entangled. In research it sits inside the wider theory of entanglement-assisted classical capacity, where a shared ebit can raise the classical throughput of a quantum channel. Newer curricula also treat it as the simplest example of a resource inequality — one ebit plus one qubit is worth two bits. Useful search terms: entanglement-assisted classical capacity, Bell-state measurement, and hyperdense coding.
